lead: A lag compensator is a first-order transfer function with a zero farther from the origin than its pole. It keeps low-frequency gain high and reduces gain at higher frequency. That relative boost lowers steady-state error or lets a designer restore phase margin after raising gain. You meet it in temperature loops, DC motor speed control and plants where accuracy matters more than speed. Design is done on the Bode plot: set the gain for error, then place a zero and pole to keep phase margin.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 steady-state error and static error constants; Unit 4 Bode plots, gain margin and phase margin; and the lead contrast in 5.4 Lead compensator design.

blocks.text: Define the lag compensator as C(s) = K<sub>c</sub>(s + z)/(s + p). K<sub>c</sub> is a real gain; z is the zero in rad/s; p is the pole in rad/s; and z > p > 0. Let β = z/p. β is greater than 1. The DC gain is C(0) = K<sub>c</sub>β. The high-frequency gain is C(∞) = K<sub>c</sub>. So low-frequency gain is β times high-frequency gain.

blocks.where: φ(ω) is the compensator phase in degrees or radians; z is the zero in rad/s; p is the pole in rad/s; ω is frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: The phase is negative at every ω because z > p. The largest lag magnitude is φ<sub>m</sub> = sin<sup>−1</sup>((β − 1)/(β + 1)). It occurs at ω<sub>m</sub> = √(zp). The phase there is −φ<sub>m</sub>. A lag compensator never adds positive phase. It trades phase for gain. For z = 0.5 rad/s and p = 0.05 rad/s, β = 10, ω<sub>m</sub> = 0.158 rad/s and φ<sub>m</sub> = 54.9°. The figure uses these values.

items: Set the open-loop gain K for the error specification using Unit 2. For a type-1 plant and a unit ramp, e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/K<sub>v</sub>, where K<sub>v</sub> is the velocity error constant.
Plot K G(jω). Record the gain crossover ω<sub>c</sub> and the phase margin.
Choose a new crossover ω<sub>c</sub>′ where the plant phase leaves enough margin. Place the lag zero about one decade below it: z = ω<sub>c</sub>′/10.
Choose β from the required low-frequency boost or the allowed high-frequency attenuation. Compute the pole as p = z/β.

Set K<sub>c</sub>. C(s) = K<sub>c</sub>(s + z)/(s + p) has DC gain K<sub>c</sub>β and high-frequency gain K<sub>c</sub>. Use K<sub>c</sub> = 1 to keep high-frequency gain unchanged and DC gain β. Use K<sub>c</sub> = 1/β to keep DC gain unchanged and high-frequency gain 1/β.
Check PM = 180° + ∠G(jω<sub>c</sub>′) + ∠C(jω<sub>c</sub>′). If PM is too small, lower z, increase β, or move ω<sub>c</sub>′ to a lower value.

sections.h3: Why it works and what it costs

blocks.text: On the Bode plot, a lag lowers high-frequency gain and moves crossover left. The plant usually has less negative phase there, so phase margin rises. If the lag raises low-frequency gain by β, then K<sub>v</sub> rises by β and ramp error falls by β. The cost is lower bandwidth, slower rise and longer settling. A lag pole very near the origin creates a slow tail in the response.

In root-locus design, a lag adds a pole-zero pair near the origin. The pole is closer to the origin than the zero. That pair raises low-frequency gain. Root-locus details are in 5.7 Compensator design using root locus and Bode plot. When one lag cannot meet both error and phase margin, use the combined section in 5.6 Lag-lead compensator design.

figure.caption: Maximum lag 54.9° at 0.158 rad/s for z = 0.5 rad/s and p = 0.05 rad/s.

spec.aria: A negative phase curve that reaches about minus 55 degrees near 0.158 radians per second and returns toward zero.

examples.question: A unity-feedback plant G(s) = 1/[s(s + 1)] must have unit-ramp steady-state error no more than 0.1. (a) Find the minimum forward gain K. (b) With K = 10, design a lag section with zero at 0.1 rad/s and high-frequency attenuation 1/7.1. Find β, p and K<sub>c</sub>, and write C(s).
steps: For the plant with gain K, K<sub>v</sub> = lim<sub>s→0</sub> s K G(s) = K. The unit-ramp error is e<sub>ss</sub> = 1/K<sub>v</sub> = 1/K.
The spec e<sub>ss</sub> ≤ 0.1 gives 1/K ≤ 0.1, so K ≥ 10. Minimum K = 10; at K = 10, e<sub>ss</sub> = 0.1.
The lag zero is z = 0.1 rad/s. High-frequency attenuation 1/7.1 means K<sub>c</sub> = 1/7.1 = 0.141 to three decimals.
The ratio β = z/p = 7.1. Thus p = z/β = 0.1/7.1 = 0.0141 rad/s to four decimals.
Check DC gain: C(0) = K<sub>c</sub>z/p = (1/7.1)(7.1) = 1.0. The loop low-frequency gain is K C(0) = 10, so e<sub>ss</sub> stays 0.1.
examples.answer: Minimum gain K = 10; β = 7.1; p = 0.0141 rad/s; K<sub>c</sub> = 0.141; C(s) = 0.141(s + 0.1)/(s + 0.0141), with maximum lag 48.9° at 0.0375 rad/s.

traps: Placing the lag zero at or near gain crossover adds too much phase lag and lowers phase margin. Put the zero about a decade below the new crossover.
Forgetting K<sub>c</sub> leaves the loop gain wrong. C(s) = (s + z)/(s + p) has DC gain β, not 1, unless β = 1.
β = z/p is greater than 1 because z > p. The pole is p = z/β, not zβ.
The maximum lag is at ω<sub>m</sub> = √(zp), not at the zero z or the pole p.
A lag does not add positive phase. It improves phase margin by lowering crossover into a region where the plant phase is less negative.

quiz.q: Define β for C(s) = K<sub>c</sub>(s + z)/(s + p) with z > p.
quiz.a: β = z/p. It is greater than 1 and equals the DC gain divided by the high-frequency gain when K<sub>c</sub> is removed.

quiz.q: Why can a lag compensator reduce steady-state error?
quiz.a: It makes low-frequency gain larger than high-frequency gain by the ratio β. That raises the velocity error constant for a type-1 loop, so ramp error falls. The phase lag must be kept small at crossover.

quiz.q: For a lag with z = 0.2 rad/s and β = 5, find p, ω<sub>m</sub> and φ<sub>m</sub>.
A lag zero is moved from 0.01ω<sub>c</sub> to 0.5ω<sub>c</sub>. What happens to phase margin?
quiz.a: More lag phase appears at crossover. Phase margin decreases, so the closed-loop response becomes more oscillatory or less damped.

quiz.q: State the formula for maximum lag magnitude and its frequency.
For C(s) = 0.1(s + 0.5)/(s + 0.05), find K<sub>c</sub>, z, p, β, DC gain and high-frequency gain.
quiz.a: K<sub>c</sub> = 0.1, z = 0.5 rad/s, p = 0.05 rad/s, β = 10. DC gain = K<sub>c</sub>β = 1. High-frequency gain = K<sub>c</sub> = 0.1.

quiz.q: Why avoid placing a lag pole extremely close to the origin?
quiz.a: A very small p gives a long time constant and a slow tail in the response. Settling time grows, and the compensator becomes hard to implement accurately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial lag compensation is often built in digital code, so the continuous zero and pole are converted to a difference equation. Loop-shaping tools in MATLAB or Octave let you drag the lag zero and pole while watching margins. Search for lag compensator Bode design, loop shaping and digital implementation of compensators. In precision motion systems, lag action is common inside PI speed and position loops.
